title: A diet from the Mediterranean
text: The Mediterranean diet began as an accident of {{1}}. In the 1950s, an American physiologist named Ancel Keys noticed that well-fed businessmen were dropping from heart attacks while villagers in southern Italy, eating little meat and much olive oil, were not. His Seven Countries Study {{2}} the association across cultures and became one of the most influential {{3}} in nutrition: the pattern — vegetables, legumes, whole grains, olive oil, fish, modest wine — was later shown in randomised trials to {{4}} the risk of major cardiovascular events by roughly thirty per cent. The diet's rivals come and go; the Mediterranean pattern {{5}}. Part of its power is that it is not a diet in the modern sense — no forbidden foods, no counting — but a default, a way of eating that survives translation into Spain, Greece, Lebanon and beyond. Researchers add a {{6}}, though: the original villagers also walked everywhere, ate slowly and napped after lunch, so the food came {{7}} in a way of life. That is harder to bottle than olive oil, and it may be the {{8}} ingredient of all.

gaps.explanation: 'an accident of geography' — where the place is and what grows there; geology = study of rocks.
'the study replicated the association' — found it again independently; rehearse = practise a performance.
'one of the most influential findings in nutrition' — established results; filings = particles filed off metal.
'trials to confirm the risk reduction' — verify it; conform takes 'to', confide takes 'in'.
'the Mediterranean pattern persists' — endures while rivals fade; insist takes 'on', consist takes 'of'.
'researchers add a warning' — a caution about over-simplifying; warden = a guardian or official.
'the food came embedded in a way of life' — set firmly inside it; enclose = surround completely.
'the essential ingredient of all' — the indispensable one; sensual = relating to physical pleasure.
